newsitem.title: USA: Lobsters, books, other goods slowed by UPS strike.
newsitem.headline: Lobsters, books, other goods slowed by UPS strike.

text.p: The UPS strike slowed deliveries of everything from air fresheners to books to lobsters Tuesday as the walkout at the nation's biggest shipper took a growing toll on thousands of businesses across the country.

With United Parcel Service's familiar brown trucks and its fleet of planes mostly idle, businesses that normally use UPS looked to other suppliers -- and good old American ingenuity -- to send goods on their way.

While UPS assigned thousands of managers and non-union workers to do the jobs that 185,000 striking drivers, sorters and loaders usually do, both sides in the dispute said the company's operations for the most part were shut down.

Companies that had planned ahead shifted deliveries to other shippers. Other merchants suffered. Some retail industry analysts said Internet merchants in particular might suffer if they had not faced a strike that disrupted deliveries before.
"We're not happy," said Susan Zumbo, who works in the sales office at Medo Industries, a Tarrytown, N.Y., maker of air fresheners and other accessories for car interiors.

"Anything we've sent out since Friday hasn't got there. Same with stuff we've been expecting here. It's in limbo out there somewhere," she said, noting Medo relies on UPS to send samples to customers and for shipments from its Baltimore factory.
In Maine, lobster dealers said the strike has crimped business since many other shippers will not accept the live crustaceans for shipment.

"If they do accept, it's at our risk and the customer's risk and it could be a two-day delivery time, which is a death sentence in the lobster business," said Peter McAleney, owner of New Meadows Lobster, a Portland company that sells lobsters to wholesalers around the world.
Other companies dealing in perishables took special measures.

Omaha Steaks of Omaha, Neb. uses Federal Express as its main shipper but was taking precautions in case Fedex becomes overloaded with orders normally handled by UPS, which normally ships 12 million packages a day and dominates most aspects of the nation's package delivery business.

"We're adding more dry ice to our packaging and informing costumers that within the next couple of days, if the strike continues, the packages could be a day late," spokeswoman Sharon Grunkin said. The company shipped about 2 million packages last year, she said.
Gateway 2000 Inc., the personal computer marketer based in North Sioux City, S.D., said it had moved shipments from UPS to other carriers over the last week or so.
"We basically weaned ourselves away from UPS to other common carriers and Fedex as well," said spokesman Greg Lund.
Traditional manufacturers were affected too.

Carpenter Technology Corp., a speciality metals maker in Reading, Pa., said shipments to its plant had dropped from 100 a day to "literally a handful," spokeswoman Katharine Marshall said. "I think yesterday we got four."
Companies said the strike would become more of a headache the longer it dragged on.

J.C. Penney Co., which normally sends 200,000 packages a day with UPS but has shifted to other air and road carriers, said so far delays have been minor. "Whether we can continue to get timely deliveries remains to be seen," spokesman Duncan Muir said. "They (the other carriers) are going to take care of us but they are all overloaded."

At Noteworthy Collection, a stationery wholesaler and printer in Atlanta, "what we did yesterday, unfortunately, was we had to go from Post Office to Post Office," said Gordon Bibbens, shipping manager.

He said Fedex would not guarantee on-time arrival while the Postal Service has limited customers to four parcels each. The company ships 35 orders a day via UPS but with the holiday season approaching that has risen to 50 a day.

On the Internet, book retailer Amazon.com's Web site alerted customers to possible delays resulting from the strike, even though it has changed to Airborne Express and the Postal Service's priority mail.

"Even with these arrangements, there may still be some delay in delivering your order," the Web site said. "Please rest assured that we will provide you with a replacement or refund should your order not arrive within the usual time frame."
